messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Vignette:
Vinh Tran was 52 when he came for treatment, a married Vietnamese American man who had spent most of his adult life working as an HVAC technician. He described the event that still sat in his mind not as a single dramatic accident but as a moment when an ordinary service call turned abruptly and unmistakably dangerous. He had been sent to inspect a commercial cooling system in a storage area behind a small manufacturing space. He remembered entering a cramped back room with poor ventilation, the kind of room he had worked in countless times before, and noticing a sharp chemical smell that did not fit with the usual odors of machinery, dust, and refrigerant. Within moments the air felt wrong. He recalled the sting in his nose and throat, the sense that his chest had tightened before he had fully understood what was happening, and the terrible realization that staying where he was might mean collapsing where no one could get to him quickly. What remained with him most strongly was not only the exposure itself but the feeling of being trapped in an enclosed room with something toxic around him that he could not see and could not control.

In the weeks afterward, Vinh found that the world no longer felt reliably safe, especially indoors. When people reassured him that a building had been cleared, or that a smell was harmless, or that he was overreacting, he could not make himself believe them. He would nod, but internally he stayed unconvinced, certain that safety was something other people claimed too easily. What frightened him most was the idea that danger could already be in the air while everyone around him acted as though nothing was wrong. He began to carry himself as if he needed to be ready at all times. He sat with his shoulders tight, jaw clenched, noticing every shift in air quality and every sensation in his body. He described himself as never fully unwinding, as though relaxing would mean letting down his guard at exactly the wrong moment.

That belief followed him into his routines at home. Before bed he checked doors and windows repeatedly, moving from one part of the house to another and then circling back because certainty never lasted. His wife would tell him the locks were set and the house was secure, but reassurance did not settle him. He needed to see the latch, test the knob, look again at the window frame. Even after returning to bed, he often felt compelled to get up once more. He did not describe a specific fear of burglary so much as a broader conviction that if he stopped monitoring the environment, something dangerous could get in or be missed. He knew the checking frustrated his wife and stretched out their evenings, but he felt unable to stop.

He also became increasingly unwilling to be alone in a room or building. If he arrived early to a job site and found himself by himself in a mechanical room, warehouse, or empty office suite, he felt a surge of alarm. The image of being trapped again with toxic air nearby came back to him with force. Over time he changed how he worked. He delayed entering spaces until someone else was present, called coworkers to stay on the line, or found reasons to wait outside. As months passed, he also began avoiding anything he thought might be stressful, not just dangerous jobs. He turned down difficult service calls, postponed tasks, and steered away from tense conversations because any increase in stress felt like too much for a system already stretched tight. At home he avoided quiet downtime as well. Sitting still in the evening, watching television, or trying to rest made him uneasy; he had come to feel that relaxation itself was dangerous, as though letting his body soften would leave him unprotected.

These habits narrowed his life. On the job, coworkers noticed he was slower to enter enclosed work areas and less willing to take assignments independently. At home, his wife saw how rarely he allowed himself to settle, and how often ordinary evenings became organized around his need to check and recheck the house. Vinh did not present these behaviors as irrational. From his point of view, they were what a careful person did after learning firsthand that a normal workday could turn hazardous in seconds.

By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the constant tension in his body and by how much effort it took to feel even minimally prepared. What finally brought him in was the recognition that he was structuring more and more of his life around not being alone, not relaxing, and not trusting anyone else’s judgment about safety. He said he was afraid that if he ever truly let his guard down, he would miss the next danger. At the same time, he hoped for some way to be in a room by himself again—at work, in his own house, anywhere—without feeling as if invisible threat was already closing in.
